statement:
Pakistan faces a persistent energy shortfall that affects households, factories, and hospitals alike. In recent years, however, solar power has emerged as an unlikely solution, spreading not through large state-led projects but through the initiative of ordinary citizens and small businesses. Falling prices for solar panels, driven mainly by manufacturing in China, have made rooftop installations affordable even for lower middle-class households, who install panels to escape frequent and costly grid outages. Unlike a centrally planned rollout, this growth has been fragmented and largely unregulated, creating challenges for utility companies that must still maintain the grid for those who cannot afford to leave it. Critics argue that this piecemeal approach benefits primarily those who can pay for the initial investment, while the poorest households, unable to afford panels, remain dependent on an increasingly strained public grid. Even so, few dispute that solar power has quietly become one of the country's fastest-growing energy sources, driven less by government policy than by ordinary people responding to necessity.

option_a: The technical process of manufacturing solar panels
option_b: How solar power has spread in Pakistan largely through individual initiative rather than government planning
option_c: The complete failure of Pakistan's electricity grid
option_d: A comparison between Pakistani and Chinese energy policy
explanation: The passage's central theme, stated in the opening and closing lines, is that solar power's growth was 'driven less by government policy than by ordinary people responding to necessity' — i.e. individual initiative, not central planning.

subject: Verbal Reasoning
statement:
When I was a boy, our small town had only one library, a single narrow room attached to the old municipal building, with a ceiling fan that groaned more than it cooled. The librarian, a stern woman named Miss Rasheeda, never smiled, yet she remembered the name of every child who borrowed a book and would set aside new arrivals for those she judged serious readers. I did not think of myself as one of them; I visited mostly to escape the afternoon heat. It was only years later, sorting through boxes after her retirement, that I found a small notebook in which she had recorded, in a careful hand, the books each of us had read and, beside certain names, brief notes such as 'ready for harder books now.' Beside my own name she had written nothing for two years, and then, quite suddenly, 'finally reading properly.' I have never been able to decide whether I became a reader because of that room, or whether she simply recognized, long before I did, that I already was one.

Q: The passage is best described as:
option_a: A formal history of a public library system
option_b: A personal recollection about a librarian's quiet influence on the narrator
option_c: An argument for building more libraries in small towns
explanation: The passage is written in the first person as a memory ('When I was a boy...') and centres on how the narrator came to see the librarian's quiet attention to his reading — a personal recollection, not a formal history, argument, or biography.
